feedback: If the sequence is reversed or collapsed, re-separate pollination (pollen arrives at the stigma) from fertilisation (cells join inside the ovule) and from seed formation.
If an asexual card is misfiled, ask whether a new plant grows straight from part of one parent without flowers or seeds. If it does, it is a clone.
activities.intendedInsight: The processes and vocabulary of plant reproduction become crisp: the parts of a flower, the ordered pollination→fertilisation→seed sequence, and the familiar asexual methods.
learnerActions: Identify and label stamen, stigma and ovary on a flower cross-section.
Put the sexual-reproduction steps in order: pollination → fertilisation → seed.
Sort example cards into asexual methods: strawberry runner, bulb, geranium cutting — naming each as producing a clone from one parent.
activities.title: Label the flower and sequence the sexual route (reference / pre-teach)

feedback: If a learner thinks only mammals reproduce, point to birds and frogs: laying and hatching an egg is reproduction too.
If a learner thinks egg-layers 'aren't really reproducing', clarify that producing a new individual is reproduction regardless of egg or live birth.
activities.intendedInsight: Animals reproduce in different ways — egg-laying and live-bearing — and both are genuine reproduction; it is not only mammals that reproduce.
learnerActions: Follow an egg-laying example (bird, frog, many insects): lay and hatch an egg.
Follow a live-bearing example (most mammals): a live birth.
Sort familiar animals into egg-laying vs live-bearing groups.
Answer: is one of these 'more' reproduction than the other? (No — producing a new individual is reproduction whether by egg or live birth.)
activities.title: Compare egg-laying and live-bearing animals

feedback: If a learner says a cutting plant will differ from its parent, revisit: a cutting from one parent → clone with the same inherited features (only growing conditions change it); sexual reproduction, usually two parents → mixed features → variation.
If a learner is unsure why a gardener chooses cuttings, connect it to the gallery: cuttings give a plant with the same inherited features as the parent, while seeds can give variety.
activities.intendedInsight: Applying the parent-number rule to a real purpose (cuttings for identical plants, seeds for variation) consolidates and extends the core idea.
learnerActions: Match examples to type: strawberry runner → asexual; apple seed → sexual.
Answer which offspring are identical to the parent, and explain why cuttings are clones.
Discuss or explain: a gardener takes a cutting to get a plant exactly like this one — why choose a cutting over a seed if you want two identical plants?
activities.title: Check and apply: why do gardeners take cuttings?
